posts.title: The system says no
posts.text:
We asked for a screen in a colour our design system does not have. The system refused, and named the token to use instead.

That refusal is what makes a design system AI-ready. Better prompts do not keep AI output on-brand. Rules that tools can read do: which components exist, what each token is for, and which names were never part of the system.

In the clip, a prompt becomes a settings page built only from the system's own components. Then a made-up token is refused, with the nearest real one.

To be clear about the demo: it runs on Demo Brand, a fictional company, and a rule-based planner stands in for the AI model. The refusal comes from the system's rules, which is why the same check works with any model.

What would your design system refuse today, if a tool asked?

#designsystems #ai #designops

posts.title: One fix, reviewed in two tools
posts.text:
In dark mode, a button's hover state looked exactly like its default. One small inconsistency. This is how we walk a client through fixing it, from the finding to Figma and code.

→ The finding names the rule it breaks: hover must differ from default in every theme.
→ Before anyone changes anything, we see what the change touches: components, Figma layers, documentation and the files AI tools read.
→ The fix is proposed once, as a token change.
→ It is reviewed in both places, as a pull request with its checks and as a Figma change, and then merged.

The figures in the clip are sample figures for Demo Brand, a fictional company, and the pull request and the Figma review are simulated in the demo. The order of the steps is the one we follow with clients.

In many teams the same bug gets fixed twice, once in each tool. Where does a fix start in yours?

#designsystems #figma #designtokens

posts.title: Every job, written down once
posts.text:
Our designers and consultants kept asking the same question: which tool do I use for this? So we wrote every job down once.

There are fourteen of them, from answering an RFP to prototyping on a client's design system. Each one says what you get, who it is for, the words people use for it, and when it is the wrong choice.

In our internal workspace you type what you need. It finds the job and tells you which of your words matched. No AI is involved in that step: it compares your words with the descriptions. The same descriptions are what an AI assistant reads when someone asks it for help.

That is the idea behind AI-ready design systems, applied to our own work: describe something once, in a form that people and tools read the same way.

Which job does your team explain again every week?

#designops #designsystems #ai
